what_it_does: When engineers write code for AI workloads, they often have many different ways to implement the same operation — different loop orders, tile sizes, memory layouts — and picking the best one for a given chip (a process called autotuning) normally requires running each option on the actual target hardware to measure speed. This is slow and expensive when real hardware is scarce. This paper proposes using instruction-accurate simulators — software programs that faithfully mimic what a real chip would do, step by step — to collect performance statistics without needing physical hardware. A machine-learning predictor then translates the simulator's statistics into an estimate of how fast the code would run on the real chip. The system was tested on three different chip families (x86 desktop, ARM mobile, and RISC-V open-source), and it reliably identified the best implementation among the top 3 percent of candidates, making the tuning process both faster and less reliant on physical hardware access.
